web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Engine — Segments, Revenue Mix & Real-World Deployments
question: How does AMD organize its business segments after its 2025 reporting consolidation, where do its revenues and operating profits actually come from, and how do real customers deploy and pay for its products?

epigraph.quote: A great technology portfolio is not a collection of isolated parts; it is a stack that solves the customer's total cost of ownership.
epigraph.author: Dr. Lisa Su, Chair & CEO, AMD (paraphrased from investor remarks)

web_blocks.title: 2.1 Segment Architecture: Three Reportable Engines (2025 Consolidation)

web_blocks.html: In Q1 2025, AMD streamlined its reporting from four segments to three reportable segments [1][2]. It merged Client and Gaming into one segment while still disclosing revenue for each line separately [1][2]. The three segments are Data Center, Client and Gaming, and Embedded [1][2]. AMD also reports an unallocated All Other corporate line. All Other holds intangible amortization ($2,254 million in FY2025; $1,629 million in 9M 2026), stock-based pay ($1,638 million in FY2025; $1,513 million in 9M 2026), and deal costs [1][2].

Data Center now drives the business. In FY2025, Data Center brought in $16,635 million, or 48.0% of total sales ($34,639 million) [1]. Across 9M 2026, Data Center jumped 86.9% YoY to $21,039 million [2]. That equaled 59.8% of total sales ($35,166 million) and 69.4% of positive segment operating profit [2]. In Q3 2026 alone, Data Center surged 97% YoY to $8,546 million (63.9% of sales) [2][3]. Segment operating margin hit 33.7% ($2,882 million), showing strong operating leverage as MI450 GPUs and 6th Gen EPYC CPUs ramped together [2][3].

web_blocks.caption: AMD Reportable Segment Revenue & Operating Income Mix (FY2023–9M 2026 & Q3 2026)
rows: All Other Operating Loss (Amort, SBC, M&A)
web_blocks.takeaway: Data Center has become AMD's dominant profit engine—reaching 63.9% of Q3 2026 revenue and 33.7% segment operating margin—while Embedded's ~40% margins are recovering and Gaming has shrunk to just 5.8% of quarterly sales.

web_blocks.html: The segment mix shift is reshaping AMD's profit profile. High-margin Data Center and Embedded units together delivered over 81% of positive segment operating income in 9M 2026 [2]. Meanwhile, low-margin Gaming has shrunk to under 6% of quarterly sales [2][3].

web_blocks.title: 2.2 Segment 1: Data Center (59.8% of 9M 2026 Revenue; $6,584M Operating Income)

web_blocks.html: Data Center sells EPYC server CPUs, Instinct AI GPUs, Pensando DPUs and AI NICs, data-center FPGAs, and Helios rack-scale systems [1][2][14]. EPYC CPUs run cloud servers, enterprise workloads, and AI host nodes. By Q1 2026, EPYC hit a record 46.2% share of x86 server CPU revenue per Mercury Research, up from 41.3% in Q4 2025 [17][21]. On the GPU side, AMD moved to a yearly release pace: MI300X in 2024, 3nm MI350/MI355X in June 2025, and HBM4-based MI450 in H2 2026 [3][14][20].

Concrete Real-World Example (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure & OpenAI Helios): Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) builds giant AI clusters for model training and inference [19]. OCI faces two major pain points: steep single-vendor GPU prices and intense rack power limits. To solve both, OCI ordered an initial 50,000-GPU supercluster built on AMD Helios racks starting in Q3 2026 [3][19]. Each liquid-cooled Helios rack packs 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs, 31 TB of HBM4 memory, 18 6th Gen EPYC 'Venice' CPUs, and Pensando 'Vulcano' AI NICs [3][14]. The rack links chips at 260 TB/s and runs open ROCm 10 software [3][14]. AMD earns revenue by selling these silicon modules, NICs, and rack designs to cloud buyers and partners like HPE, Lenovo, and Sanmina [2][3][8]. OpenAI and Meta also signed binding 1-gigawatt initial MI450 deals within 6-gigawatt frameworks, backed by equity warrants [6][7].

web_blocks.title: 2.3 Segment 2: Client and Gaming (31.8% of 9M 2026 Revenue; $1,730M Operating Income)

web_blocks.html: Client and Gaming pairs two very different units [1]. Client ($10,640 million in FY2025; $8,896 million in 9M 2026, +17.9% YoY) sells Ryzen PC chips, AI PC APUs, and Threadripper workstations [1][2][3]. Gaming ($3,910 million in FY2025; $2,272 million in 9M 2026, -25.9% YoY) makes semi-custom chips for PlayStation and Xbox plus Radeon graphics cards [1][2]. As current consoles age, Gaming sales dropped 40% YoY to $773 million in Q3 2026 [2][3]. That decline pulled segment operating margin down from 19.6% in FY2025 to 15.5% in 9M 2026 [1][2].

Concrete Real-World Example (Commercial AI Laptops & Consoles): A large software firm refreshing 10,000 developer laptops wants staff to run local AI coding models offline without draining batteries. PC makers like HP and Lenovo buy AMD's Ryzen AI Max PRO 400 Series chips for these mobile workstations and Halo desktops [3]. Each chip pairs Zen CPU cores, Radeon graphics, and an XDNA NPU on unified memory. AMD books revenue per chip shipped to OEMs on forecast purchase orders, earning stronger margins on commercial PRO lines [1][3]. In Gaming, Sony co-funds semi-custom chip design and buys millions of lower-margin console APUs over a seven-year cycle [1][2].

web_blocks.title: 2.4 Segment 3: Embedded (8.4% of 9M 2026 Revenue; $1,177M Operating Income)

web_blocks.html: Built on the 2022 Xilinx deal, Embedded sells Versal adaptive SoCs, FPGAs, System-on-Modules, and embedded CPUs [1][2]. A tough two-year customer inventory glut cut sales from $5,321 million in FY2023 to $3,454 million in FY2025 [1]. In 2026, Embedded bounced back cleanly. Nine-month sales rose 18.2% YoY to $2,959 million, and Q3 2026 jumped 29.4% YoY to $1,109 million [2][3]. Operating margin hit 40.8% ($453 million)—AMD's highest segment margin—thanks to sticky 7-to-15-year industrial design wins [2][3].

Concrete Real-World Example (Space Satellites & Self-Driving Trucks): Aerospace firms building orbital satellites cannot use standard chips because space radiation corrupts memory. They buy AMD's radiation-tolerant Versal AI Core XQRVC1902 adaptive SoC, which began sampling in Q3 2026 [3]. It runs reliably for up to 15 years in space and lets engineers reprogram its hardware logic from Earth [3]. On the ground, Kodiak AI uses embedded EPYC CPUs in its autonomous freight trucks to fuse sensor data in real time [3]. AMD sells these chips directly and through specialized distributors like Avnet, earning high-margin multi-year revenue streams [1][3].

Note 4 of the FY2025 Form 10-K breaks down revenue by customer billing location [1]. The United States led at $11,363 million (32.8% of sales) [1]. China including Hong Kong ranked second at $7,751 million (22.4%), followed by Taiwan ($5,186 million, 15.0%) and Singapore ($4,284 million, 12.4%) [1]. Other regions added $6,055 million (17.5%) [1]. No single customer reached 10% of total revenue in FY2025 or FY2024, down from one 18% buyer in FY2023 [1]. Still, one customer held 11% of year-end FY2025 receivables, and hyperscaler concentration will likely climb as MI450 scales [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: Nearly 22.4% of FY2025 revenue was billed to China and Hong Kong, making U.S. BIS export controls a recurring structural risk even as U.S. hyperscaler AI deployments accelerate in 2026.

web_blocks.html: While Taiwan and Singapore billing figures largely reflect Asian ODMs assembling global servers and PCs, the 22.4% China and Hong Kong share creates direct policy risk [1]. Any new U.S. export rule can freeze shipments overnight, as seen with the MI308 ban in April 2025 [9].

book_paragraphs: To understand how AMD actually makes money today, you and I should throw out the old mental model of AMD as a PC-and-Xbox chipmaker. Beginning in early 2025, management consolidated its reporting into three clean segments: Data Center, Client and Gaming, and Embedded. Look at the third quarter of 2026, and the transformation jumps off the page. Data Center generated 8.55 billion dollars in a single quarter—nearly 64 percent of the entire company's sales and more than two-thirds of its segment operating profits.

Let's walk inside each of these three engines and see a concrete, real-world customer transaction from start to finish. First, step into a massive cloud data center run by Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Oracle's problem is simple to state and brutally hard to solve: its AI customers need tens of thousands of GPUs wired together to train and run frontier models, yet relying on a single GPU supplier crushes Oracle's margins and leaves it hostage to one vendor's allocation queue.

In late 2025 and 2026, Oracle turned to AMD for a 50,000-GPU supercluster built around AMD's Helios rack-scale platform. Inside every liquid-cooled Helios rack sit 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs sharing 31 terabytes of high-bandwidth HBM4 memory, orchestrated by 18 sixth-generation EPYC Venice server CPUs and wired together with Pensando networking cards running open ROCm 10 software. AMD does not just sell a bare silicon die anymore; it sells the full compute, networking, and reference-rack blueprint. When those racks ship, Data Center operating margins expand rapidly—jumping from 21.7 percent in 2025 to 33.7 percent in the third quarter of 2026.

book_subsections.title: Client & Gaming: Commercial AI PCs Carrying a Fading Console Cycle
paragraphs: Next, look at AMD's second segment, Client and Gaming, which brought in 11.2 billion dollars across the first nine months of 2026. Inside that combined bucket, two very different stories are playing out. The Client side—Ryzen laptop and desktop chips—grew nearly 18 percent year-over-year to 8.9 billion dollars. Picture a global software company refreshing ten thousand developer laptops from HP or Lenovo. Engineers want to run local AI models right on their desks without paying cloud API fees or leaking proprietary code. HP and Lenovo buy AMD's Ryzen AI Max PRO 400 processors, which pack CPU, GPU, and neural processing cores onto unified memory, paying AMD healthy commercial prices per chip.

The Gaming side tells the opposite story. AMD builds the custom brain inside Sony's PlayStation and Microsoft's Xbox consoles. Early in a console generation, those semi-custom chips deliver billions in predictable revenue. Late in the cycle, volumes inevitably fade. In the third quarter of 2026, Gaming revenue dropped 40 percent year-over-year to 773 million dollars, now less than six percent of total company sales. That shrinkage is actually healthy for AMD's long-term quality, because low-margin console silicon is being steadily replaced by high-margin data center compute.

book_subsections.title: Inside a Helios Rack: Why AMD Now Sells Systems, Not Just Chips
paragraphs: Pause and picture what actually changed inside AMD's Data Center division between 2024 and 2026. Back in 2024, when AMD sold Instinct MI300X GPUs, hyperscalers bought bare accelerator modules and had to spend months designing their own motherboards, power delivery, liquid cooling manifolds, and cluster networking. That engineering friction slowed adoption and handed NVIDIA a massive time-to-market advantage with its turnkey NVL72 racks.

Acquiring ZT Systems' rack-design team in March 2025—and divesting ZT's low-margin assembly factories to Sanmina seven months later—solved that bottleneck. Today, when Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, or Anthropic orders AMD Helios, they receive a pre-validated, liquid-cooled AI supercomputer rack packing 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs, 31 terabytes of HBM4 memory, 18 sixth-generation EPYC Venice CPUs, and Pensando Vulcano networking cards moving data at 260 terabytes per second inside the rack. Because AMD captures silicon value across the GPU, the host CPU, and the network interface card simultaneously, Data Center operating margin leaped to 33.7 percent in Q3 2026.

book_subsections.title: How Client, Gaming & Embedded Balance—or Drag—the Portfolio
paragraphs: While Data Center steals the headlines, you should always check the health of AMD's other two segments because they generate steady cash flow and diversify customer exposure. In Client, AMD's Ryzen mobile and commercial PRO processors grew 17.9 percent across the first nine months of 2026 to 8.9 billion dollars. Commercial laptops sold to Fortune 500 IT departments carry far stickier margins than consumer PCs, yet desktop unit share still whipsaws quarter to quarter whenever Intel floods the channel with discounted chips—as happened in Q3 2026.

Gaming, meanwhile, is now a tiny late-cycle tail—down 40 percent year-over-year to 773 million dollars in Q3 2026 as PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X age. Embedded is the quiet hero: selling radiation-hardened Versal space chips and industrial FPGAs at 40.8 percent operating margins gives AMD an annuity-like profit cushion that does not depend on consumer PC moods or gaming console calendars.

book_subsections.title: Embedded: The Quiet 40-Percent-Margin Crown Jewel
paragraphs: Finally, never overlook AMD's third segment: Embedded. Inherited largely from the 2022 Xilinx acquisition, Embedded sells programmable FPGAs and adaptive chips into aerospace, defense, industrial robotics, telecommunications, and autonomous vehicles. Think about an aerospace contractor building a low-earth-orbit satellite. You cannot send a technician into orbit with a screwdriver if communication protocols change five years after launch. So the contractor buys AMD's space-grade Versal adaptive SoC—engineered to survive 15 years of radiation while allowing engineers to reprogram its hardware logic from the ground. Meanwhile, autonomous freight company Kodiak AI runs embedded EPYC processors inside self-driving trucks to fuse radar and camera feeds in real time.

Embedded endured a painful two-year customer inventory hangover after 2023, falling from 5.3 billion dollars to 3.45 billion dollars in 2025. By the third quarter of 2026, the clouds cleared: revenue jumped 29 percent year-over-year to 1.11 billion dollars, and segment operating margin snapped back to 40.8 percent—the highest profitability of any division at AMD.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: When you look at AMD's geographic table, keep one critical caveat in mind. China and Hong Kong accounted for 7.75 billion dollars, or 22.4 percent of total FY2025 billing revenue. While part of that reflects Asian server and PC assembly for Western buyers, a meaningful slice is direct Chinese demand subject to sudden U.S. Commerce Department export rules—just as we saw with the 800-million-dollar MI308 hit in 2025. Diversification into U.S. hyperscalers helps, yet geopolitical friction remains a permanent tax on AMD's addressable market.
